CV Defense Dossier#

BraTS: Controlled A/B in post-treatment glioma segmentation#

This document defends one CV entry, phrase by phrase. Every noun, number, and qualifier in the four bullets below is unpacked into: the claim, what it means, the evidence (a plot, table, or statistic from the committed run logs), where to verify it, and the interview question it invites — answered honestly, including where the work is deliberately limited.

The CV entry being defended#

BraTS: Controlled A/B in post-treatment glioma segmentation

  • Reproduced a defective glioma-segmentation pipeline as a controlled A/B to isolate cause from model.
  • Curated 700 BraTS-2024 post-treatment glioma MRIs (3 modalities) into a stratified 490/105/105 split.
  • Fixed 9 pipeline defects with a 1.98M-param MONAI 3D U-Net held byte-identical across the two tracks.
  • Lifted held-out mean foreground Dice from 0.349 to 0.670 (+0.321 ± 0.013, 3 seeds); rarest class +0.457.

The verdict in one line

Every quantitative claim in the entry is reproducible from committed artifacts, and the central causal claim — the pipeline, not the model, caused the gap — is licensed by holding a 1,983,069-parameter network byte-identical across both arms. The honest limitations (voxel-wise not lesion-wise Dice; a small model on a resampled mirror; n = 3 seeds on one test split) are stated in §5 rather than hidden, which is itself part of the defense.

How to read this#

Each of the four sections below takes one bullet and walks its phrases in order. Three kinds of box recur:

The one-liner

The single sentence that defends a phrase if you remember nothing else.

Watch out

Where the claim is easy to overstate — the boundary you must not cross when talking about it.

Interview question

The sharpest question the phrase invites, with a crisp, honest answer.

A companion document — the Explainer (explainer.html) — carries the from-scratch theory (what a glioma is, how MRI works, how a U-Net and the Dice loss are derived). This dossier cross-references it as §N rather than repeating those derivations; it stays focused on defending the claims.

Watch out — the metric caveat that governs the whole entry

Every Dice number here is voxel-wise Dice, not the BraTS lesion-wise challenge score. The numbers are internally consistent for an A/B comparison but are not comparable to leaderboards. Quote the delta, not the absolute level (see §4 and §5).

1. Bullet 1 — "Reproduced a defective pipeline as a controlled A/B to isolate cause from model"#

This bullet makes a causal claim — that a documented segmentation failure was caused by the pipeline, not by an inadequate network. A causal claim is only as good as the experiment that licenses it, so every phrase below is really a defense of experimental design. The three phrases unpack in order: what was reproduced (a pipeline's behaviour, honestly sourced and faithfully — not weakly — reproduced), how it was compared (a controlled A/B where exactly one thing moves), and why the comparison is attributable (a byte-identical network is what turns a difference into a cause).

"Reproduced … a defective … pipeline"#

Claim. "Reproduced a defective glioma-segmentation pipeline." The object of the verb is the data pipeline's behaviour — its label handling, normalisation, sampling, loss, and checkpoint-selection — not a set of trained weights. No original weights were reused; the pathology was re-implemented in PyTorch/MONAI and shown to reproduce.

What it means — honest provenance first. The reference was a Colab export, unet_cc.py, whose header literally reads "Copy of Untitled7.ipynb … Automatically generated by Colab." That header is itself a tell: the file is a copy of an unnamed shared notebook, and it carries a BraTS-2020-era label remap forward onto 2024 data — the remap is defect D7 (it merges the resection cavity into enhancing tumour, collapsing the problem to 4 classes). The file has no author, no README, and no LICENSE. It was not redistributed; only its behaviour was reproduced. This matters for the honesty of the claim: "reproduced" means reproduced a documented pathology from re-written code, not forked someone's repo and reran it.

Evidence — this is a faithful reproduction, not a strawman. A reproduction is only defensible if it recreates the documented pathology rather than an easy-to-beat caricature. Track A does exactly that. On validation it reaches a voxel accuracy of 0.991 while its mean foreground Dice is only 0.320, and the rarest class, NETC, sits at Dice 0.009 — a near-total miss. That accuracy-vs-Dice divergence is the pathology: a model that predicts "background" almost everywhere scores 99% of voxels correct while segmenting essentially nothing. The "best" checkpoint was selected at epochs 18–22 on validation accuracy, which is defect D4 operating as designed.

Watch out — every Dice here is voxel-wise

These are voxel-wise Dice scores, not the BraTS lesion-wise challenge metric. They are internally consistent for an A/B comparison but are not comparable to leaderboards. Throughout this bullet, the load-bearing quantity is the contrast between the arms, never the absolute level.

Verify. The fidelity numbers (val acc 0.991, val mean-fg 0.320, NETC 0.009, checkpoint epochs 18–22) are plotted in reports/figures/dossier/track_a_fidelity.png and recomputed in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py. The provenance is quotable from the reference file header — unet_cc.py opens with "Copy of Untitled7.ipynb … Automatically generated by Colab" — though that file is local-only (it has no license and was purged from the public repository, so it is not redistributed). The nine defects and their exact fixes are catalogued in §20 of the Explainer.

Interview question

"Isn't Track A a strawman you built specifically so it would lose?" No — and it is checkable. Each defect Track A carries is traced to a real line of the reference code (D1 = a cv2.resize bilinear interpolation on the label volume; D4 = checkpoint selection on accuracy; D5 = global-max normalisation; and so on — see §20). Track A reproduces the documented pathology: 99.1% voxel accuracy with 0.320 mean-fg Dice, the classic "predicts background" collapse. If anything I was more generous than the reference, not less: the reference is a 4-class contract that merges the resection cavity into enhancing tumour (defect D7), which quietly deletes one hard class from the scoring. I kept the full 5-class problem, so Track A is graded on strictly harder terms than the original it reproduces.

Interview question

"Whose code did you reproduce, and did you have the right to?" It was an unattributed Colab export (unet_cc.py, header: "Copy of Untitled7.ipynb … Automatically generated by Colab") — itself a copy of an unnamed shared notebook, with no author, no README, and no LICENSE. Because there is no license and no clear owner, I did not redistribute it and reused no original weights. What I reproduced is its behaviour, re-implemented from scratch in PyTorch/MONAI, and I document the provenance honestly rather than claiming authorship of the pipeline it came from.

"controlled A/B"#

Claim. "as a controlled A/B." A controlled experiment is one in which exactly one thing changes between the two arms and everything else is held fixed, so that any measured difference can be assigned to that one thing.

What it means. Here the single moving part is the data-and-training pipeline — bundled as three coupled changes that always travel together: the data pipeline (label resampling, normalisation, patch sampling), the loss, and the checkpoint-selection rule. Track A carries the defective versions (it reproduces D1, D3, D4, D5, D6, D9); Track B carries the fixes. Everything an experimenter would otherwise be tempted to also improve is frozen: the network architecture (byte-identical, see below), the data split (the same fixed 490/105/105, seed 42), and the seeds protocol (both arms trained over the same 3 seeds). Two defects are deliberately outside the A/B to keep it clean: D8 (no normalisation layers in the net) is held constant on both tracks — it is not part of the comparison — and D2 (a Dice metric shape/index bug) is fixed on both so that the yardstick itself is trustworthy in both arms. D7 (the 4→5-class contract) is enforced on both so both arms are scored on the same 5 classes.

Evidence — the defect ladder. The set of changes is not an unordered pile; it is a ladder from raw pathology to corrected pipeline, each rung a named defect with a named fix. Making the bundle explicit is what makes the A/B controlled — an interviewer can see that nothing improved silently.

The one-liner

Change the pipeline, freeze the model, split, and seeds — so the only thing that can explain the gap is the pipeline.

Verify. The defect-by-defect ladder and which arm carries which rung live in §20 of the Explainer and in the diagram source note/diagrams/s20_defect_ladder.mmd. The frozen split (490/105/105, stratified by RC presence, seed 42) is asserted at data-load time and reproduced in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py.

Watch out — a bundle is one variable only if it always moves together

The pipeline change is three coupled edits (data, loss, checkpoint rule). That is legitimately "one variable" for an A/B only because they are never varied independently — I do not claim to isolate the loss from the sampler from the selection rule. The bullet's causal claim is at the level of "the pipeline," not "the DiceCE loss specifically." Anyone who wants per-defect attribution needs an ablation, which this A/B does not provide.

Interview question

"How is bundling several changes into one arm a controlled experiment — isn't that many variables at once?" It is controlled at the resolution the claim is made: pipeline vs. model. The three edits (data handling, loss, checkpoint-selection) are treated as one variable because they always move together and are never varied independently, while the genuinely tempting confounders — architecture, data split, and seed protocol — are each held fixed. So the experiment cleanly attributes the delta to "the pipeline as a whole." What it deliberately does not do is attribute the delta to any single defect; that would require a per-defect ablation, and I am careful not to over-claim that resolution.

"to isolate cause from model"#

Claim. "to isolate cause from model." The purpose of freezing the architecture is to make the observed gap unattributable to the network — to separate the cause (pipeline) from a possible confound (a better model).

What it means — the byte-identical network is what licenses the causal claim. Both arms instantiate the same network: a MONAI UNet, spatial_dims=3, in_channels=3, out_channels=5, channels (16, 32, 64, 128, 256), num_res_units=0, dropout 0.1 — 1,983,069 trainable parameters, identical down to the parameter count on both tracks. Because the function class is fixed, the network cannot be the reason Track B wins.

Evidence and the counterfactual. The whole causal argument is a counterfactual: if Track B had also been given a stronger network, then the improvement would be jointly caused by architecture and pipeline, and the two contributions would be confounded — unattributable. The bullet would then have to read "a better pipeline and a better model did better," which is not a finding, just a bigger bet. By holding the 1,983,069-parameter network byte-identical, the only thing left that can explain a difference is the pipeline. (The magnitude of that difference — held-out mean-fg Dice 0.349 → 0.670, Δ = +0.321 ± 0.013 over 3 seeds — is defended in §4; here the point is only that it is attributable.)

The one-liner

Same net, same split, same seeds — so a difference in output is, by construction, a difference the pipeline made.

Verify. The identical architecture and the 1,983,069-parameter count are printed at model-build time on both tracks and tabulated in reports/figures/dossier/param_breakdown.png; the count is recomputed in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py. That both arms share one split and one seed protocol is asserted in the data module and reproduced in the same script.

Watch out — 'byte-identical network' is a claim about the architecture, not the weights

The two arms share an identical function class and initialisation protocol, not identical learned weights — the weights necessarily differ because the training signal (loss, sampling, data) differs. That is the point: same net, different pipeline, different weights as a consequence of the pipeline. Do not overstate it as "identical models."

Interview question

"How do you know it's the pipeline and not the model?" Because the model is the one thing I refused to change. Both arms are the exact same MONAI 3D U-Net — 1,983,069 parameters, identical channels, strides, and dropout — trained on the same fixed 490/105/105 split under the same 3-seed protocol. The only difference between the arms is the data-and-training pipeline (labels, normalisation, sampling, loss, checkpoint rule). Under those conditions the Track A → Track B gap has no architectural degree of freedom to hide in. The counterfactual makes it concrete: had I also upgraded Track B's network, the delta would be confounded by architecture plus pipeline and I could not claim either as the cause — which is precisely the mistake this design exists to avoid.

2. Bullet 2 — "Curated 700 BraTS-2024 post-treatment glioma MRIs (3 modalities) into a stratified 490/105/105 split"#

This bullet is the data-provenance claim. It has to survive the two questions any careful reviewer asks about a medical-imaging dataset: where did it come from, and what did you actually do to it? The honest answer is that I did no manual annotation whatsoever — "curated" here means quality-control, contract-checking, and a reproducible split, all recomputable from committed artifacts. Everything below is designed to make that boundary explicit rather than let the word "curated" over-claim.

The one-liner

I did not label a single voxel. I verified 700 already-labelled volumes against a strict integer label contract, confirmed they were the post-treatment 2024 vintage, and cut them into a frozen, stratified 490/105/105 split at seed 42 — a data-engineering claim, not an annotation claim.

"Curated 700"#

Claim. "Curated 700 … MRIs." The dataset is 700 cases pulled from a Kaggle mirror (i212385nomanarif/2024-brats-glioma) of the BraTS-2024 post-treatment glioma collection (BraTS-GLI).

What it means. "Curated" is doing a specific, limited job here and it is essential not to inflate it. It does not mean I hand-annotated the tumours — expert neuroradiologist segmentation of a glioma takes hours per case and is exactly the labour the BraTS challenge organisers already funded. What I did is curation in the data-engineering sense:

  1. Verified the label contract. Every segmentation mask was checked to be strictly integer-valued with values a subset of \(\{0,1,2,3,4\}\) — i.e. no stray floats, no out-of-range indices, no silent class introduced by an upstream resample. This is not a formality: defect D1 (§20) is precisely a case where a bilinear resize of a label volume invents fractional, then rounded, phantom classes. Contract-checking at load time is what catches that.
  2. Confirmed the vintage (that these really are post-treatment 2024 scans, not a pre-operative set mislabelled — see the next subsection).
  3. Gzip-on-arrival. The mirror ships raw .nii; each volume was gzip-compressed on ingest to keep the on-disk footprint manageable (the recorded working subset is ~4.9 GB on disk for its slice).

Evidence & Verify. The dataset identity, case count, and the resampled geometry caveat are recorded in the committed provenance stamp reports/data_provenance.json ("dataset": "kaggle:i212385nomanarif/2024-brats-glioma", modalities_kept: [t2f, t1c, t2w], a content SHA-256 prefix, and an explicit geometry note). The label-contract audit — the per-label present-counts across all 700 cases — is regenerated by scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py and frozen in reports/dossier_facts.json under stratification.label_present.

Interview question

"Does 'curated' mean you annotated the scans?" No — and I'm careful to say so. The expert voxel-level segmentations were produced by the BraTS-2024 organisers and their neuroradiology annotators; I never drew a mask. My curation was quality control: I verified every mask is integer-valued with labels \(\subseteq\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), confirmed the post-treatment vintage, gzip-compressed on ingest, and produced a reproducible split. If I claimed to have annotated 700 gliomas, that would be false; the CV verb is "curated" precisely to stay honest about that boundary.

"BraTS-2024"#

Claim. "BraTS-2024." The source is the 2024 edition of the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) challenge.

What it means. BraTS is the long-running international benchmark for brain-tumour segmentation: the organisers release multi-parametric MRI volumes with expert consensus labels and score submissions on held-out data. Editions are versioned by year, and the label ontology has drifted over time — which matters a great deal here (a BraTS-2020-era label remap dragged onto 2024 data is exactly defect D7, §20). The 2024 edition is significant because it introduced the post-treatment glioma task (BraTS-GLI) — the first BraTS to ask models to segment brains after surgery and therapy rather than at diagnosis. Choosing the 2024 vintage is therefore the whole point of the project: it is what makes the resection-cavity class (label 4) exist at all.

Evidence & Verify. The dataset string in both reports/splits.json and reports/data_provenance.json names the 2024 BraTS-GLI mirror. For anything absolute about the challenge — its official case counts, geometry, or leaderboard scoring — I do not trust the community mirror; reports/data_provenance.json carries the citation to the official BraTS 2024 paper (cite: "BraTS 2024 (de Verdier et al., arXiv:2405.18368) — PARTIAL community mirror"), and flags itself as a partial mirror.

Watch out — mirror geometry

The mirror's volumes are 182×218×182, a resampled, MNI-like grid — not the native BraTS geometry of 240×240×155. Someone quoting the mirror as if it were the canonical release would be wrong. This is recorded verbatim in reports/data_provenance.json ("geometry": "182x218x182 … native BraTS is 240x240x155 — provenance caveat").

Interview question

"Is a community Kaggle mirror trustworthy enough to build on?" For an internal, self-consistent A/B — yes, with caveats I state openly. The mirror is a resampled copy (182×218×182 MNI-like, not the native 240×240×155), so it is fine for comparing two pipelines against each other but I would not benchmark it against the official leaderboard. For any absolute claim about BraTS-2024, I cite the official paper (de Verdier et al., arXiv:2405.18368), not the mirror. The mirror's identity and its exact resampling caveat are pinned in reports/data_provenance.json, including a content hash so the specific bytes I used are reproducible.

"post-treatment glioma"#

Claim. "post-treatment glioma." These are gliomas imaged after clinical intervention — surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy — not at initial diagnosis.

What it means. A glioma is a tumour arising from the brain's glial (support) cells (the biology is derived from scratch in the explainer, §1). "Post-treatment" changes the segmentation problem fundamentally. After a neurosurgeon resects a tumour, the removed tissue leaves a resection cavity (RC) — a fluid- or blood-filled void with surgical margins — and the surrounding brain shows treatment effects: post-radiation gliosis, blood products, and enhancement that can mimic residual or recurrent tumour. Concretely, the post-treatment label set adds the RC class (label 4) on top of the pre-operative tumour sub-regions. This is harder than the pre-operative task for two reasons: (a) there are more, and more confusable, classes to separate — enhancing tumour vs. treatment-related enhancement look alike on a single sequence; and (b) the anatomy is distorted by the surgery itself, so the tidy tumour-plus-oedema geometry of a pre-op scan no longer holds.

The five labels in this ontology are: 0 background, 1 NETC (non-enhancing tumour core), 2 SNFH (surrounding non-enhancing FLAIR hyperintensity / oedema), 3 ET (enhancing tumour), 4 RC (resection cavity).

Evidence. How do I know the set is post-treatment and not a mislabelled pre-op batch? The label-presence audit answers it. Enhancing tumour (label 3, ET) is present in 579 of 700 cases, and the resection cavity (label 4, RC) in 580 of 700. A pre-operative BraTS set uses the label vocabulary \(\{0,1,2,4\}\) without a genuine RC; the co-presence of both a live ET class and an RC class across the corpus is the signature of the post-treatment 2024 vintage and rules out a mislabelled pre-op set.

Verify. These counts are the label_present block of reports/dossier_facts.json ({"1": 353, "2": 700, "3": 579, "4": 580} over 700 cases), regenerated by scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py.

Interview question

"How do you actually know these are post-treatment scans and not a pre-op set?" By auditing the labels rather than trusting the folder name. Enhancing tumour (label 3) appears in 579/700 cases and a resection cavity (label 4) in 580/700 — a pre-operative BraTS set would carry no genuine RC class. The presence of a real RC class across ~83% of the corpus is exactly the post-treatment signature, and it's recomputable from reports/dossier_facts.json. That audit is also what lets me assert the 5-class contract at load time and catch the reference's 4-class remap (D7).

"MRIs (3 modalities)"#

Claim. "MRIs (3 modalities)." Each case is a multi-parametric MRI: three co-registered sequences used as the three input channels — t2f (T2-FLAIR), t1c (post-contrast T1), and t2w (T2).

What it means. No single MRI sequence shows a whole glioma. MRI is parametric: by changing the acquisition you make different tissues bright, and each tumour sub-region is best seen on a different sequence (the physics is derived in the explainer, §1). Roughly: t1c (T1 after gadolinium contrast) lights up enhancing tumour where the blood–brain barrier is broken; t2f (FLAIR, which suppresses free fluid) reveals the SNFH / oedema halo; t2w delineates fluid and cavity boundaries. Feeding all three as channels lets the network exploit their complementary contrast — this is why the input has in_channels = 3 (§3).

Why three, not four? The native T1 sequence (t1n) available in the release was deliberately dropped, matching the reference pipeline's channel selection. t1n carries the least sub-region-specific information once t1c is present (t1c is the same weighting plus contrast), so the marginal signal it adds is small relative to the extra I/O and memory per volume. Holding the channel set identical to the reference also keeps the A/B honest — the two tracks differ in pipeline, never in inputs.

Evidence & Verify. reports/data_provenance.json records "modalities_kept": ["t2f", "t1c", "t2w"] and "label": "seg"; the network's in_channels = 3 is fixed in configs/base.yaml and reflected in the committed parameter count (§3).

Watch out

"3 modalities" is a modelling choice, not a limit of the data — the mirror also ships t1n. Don't imply the dataset only has three sequences; it has four and I use three, on purpose, to match the reference.

Interview question

"Why throw away t1n — isn't more input always better?" Not for free. t1n is native T1; t1c is the same weighting after contrast, so once you have t1c the extra sub-region-specific signal in t1n is marginal, while it costs an extra channel of I/O and memory per patch. More importantly, the reference pipeline used exactly {t2f, t1c, t2w}, and the whole project is a controlled A/B — matching its inputs byte-for-byte is what lets me attribute the Dice gap to the nine pipeline fixes rather than to a richer input. The kept-modality list is pinned in reports/data_provenance.json.

"stratified" + "490/105/105 split"#

Claim. "a stratified 490/105/105 split." The 700 cases are partitioned 70/15/15 into train (490), validation (105), and test (105), stratified by resection-cavity presence, with the partition frozen at seed 42.

What it means. A split separates the data by role so that the number you report is honest. Stratified sampling means the partition is drawn so that a chosen class-balance is preserved across all three subsets, rather than left to the luck of a random shuffle. Here the stratification variable is a per-case binary: does this case contain a resection cavity (label 4)? The RC class is the defining, and imbalanced, feature of the post-treatment task (present in ~83% of cases), so a naive random split could leave the small test set with an unrepresentative RC rate and make the test Dice a lottery. Stratifying on RC presence removes that particular source of split-luck.

The result is striking and is the single best evidence that the stratification actually fired: the resection cavity is present in 82.9% of cases in train, validation, AND test — identical to three significant figures. Concretely the RC counts are 406/490, 87/105, and 87/105, each equal to \(87/105 = 406/490 = 82.857\% \approx 82.9\%\).

The three roles are not interchangeable — each subset is touched a different number of times, which is what keeps the final number honest:

Split n Fraction Role How often it's touched
train 490 70% updates the network weights (back-propagation) every optimiser step
val 105 15% selects the checkpoint (no gradient flows) every epoch, read-only
test 105 15% the held-out estimate reported in the CV entry once, after everything is frozen

The seed matters as much as the ratio: fixing seed 42 makes the exact 490/105/105 membership deterministic and identical across every run and both tracks. Track A and Track B therefore see the same 490 training cases and are judged on the same 105 test cases — without that guarantee the +0.321 voxel-wise Dice delta (§4) could be an artefact of a friendlier split rather than of the pipeline fixes.

Verify. The complete membership — seed, stratify key, and the per-split RC counts — is committed as reports/splits.json ("seed": 42, "stratify": "rc_presence", train {n:490, rc:406}, val {n:105, rc:87}, test {n:105, rc:87}), and it lists every case ID by name so the partition is auditable case-by-case. The identical 82.857% figure and the figure above are regenerated by scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py → reports/dossier_facts.json (stratification.splits).

Interview question

"Why stratify, and why freeze the split?" I stratify on resection-cavity presence because RC is the defining, imbalanced feature of the post-treatment task; a random 15% test set could easily land with an unrepresentative RC rate and turn the reported Dice into split-luck. Stratifying pins RC presence to an identical 82.9% in all three subsets (406/490, 87/105, 87/105), verifiable in reports/splits.json. I freeze the split at seed 42 so both tracks train on the same 490 cases and are scored on the same 105 — that's what licenses attributing the +0.321 delta to the nine pipeline fixes rather than to a luckier partition. Val selects the checkpoint; test is touched exactly once, at the very end.

Watch out — what the split does not buy

Stratifying by RC presence balances one binary. It does not balance the rarer classes (NETC is present in only 353/700 cases) or scanner/site distribution, and it says nothing about generalisation beyond this mirror. The honest uncertainty in the headline result is a single 105-case test set on one resampled mirror — a point made in full in §5, not hidden here.

3. Bullet 3 — "Fixed 9 pipeline defects with a 1.98M-param MONAI 3D U-Net held byte-identical across the two tracks"#

This bullet is the experimental design in one line. It makes three separable promises: that nine concrete defects were identified and fixed, that the fixes — not some architecture change — are what moved the score, and that the network was frozen so tightly across the comparison that it cannot be the confound. Everything below is written so an interviewer can check each promise against a committed file.

The one-liner

Change the pipeline, freeze the network. Nine defects are the independent variable; the 1.98M-parameter U-Net is the controlled variable, held byte-identical so the A→B delta belongs to the fixes and nothing else.

"Fixed 9 pipeline defects"#

Claim. "Fixed 9 pipeline defects" — a catalogue of nine specific engineering errors, labelled D1–D9, that the reference pipeline either committed or left unhandled.

What it means. The reference code was a Colab export (unet_cc.py, header "Copy of Untitled7.ipynb … Automatically generated by Colab") with no author, README, or LICENSE, carrying a BraTS-2020-era label remap onto 2024 data. Rather than "improve" it globally, each defect was isolated so its effect could be attributed. Six of the nine are reproduced faithfully in Track A and only fixed in Track B — those are the independent variable of the A/B. The other three are handled specially and are noted as such below, because pretending they were part of the A/B would overstate the result.

# Defect (reference behaviour) Fix (Track B) Why it matters A/B status
D1 Bilinear cv2.resize (INTER_LINEAR) on the label volume → fractional labels invent/destroy voxels Nearest-neighbour resampling for labels Interpolating a categorical mask fabricates classes; it inflates NETC to 105/105 and ET to 100/105 GT-present cases vs the honest 48 and 85 Reproduced in A
D2 Per-class Dice shape/index bug → original logs untrustworthy Correct MONAI DiceMetric If you can't measure per-class Dice correctly you can't compare tracks at all Fixed on BOTH (you must measure right to compare)
D3 Class imbalance unhandled; plain cross-entropy DiceCELoss + class-balanced patch sampling CE is dominated by the ~99% background voxels, so the net minimises loss by predicting background → near-zero minority Dice Reproduced in A
D4 Checkpoint selected on validation voxel accuracy Select on mean foreground Dice Accuracy of 0.991 is reachable by predicting all-background; it picks a degenerate checkpoint (epochs 18–22) whose mean-fg Dice is only 0.320 Reproduced in A
D5 Global-max normalisation X / max(X) Per-modality z-score over brain (nonzero) voxels One bright voxel rescales the whole volume and flattens cross-modality contrast the network needs Reproduced in A
D6 Non-uniform slice stride int(j·2.5), 48 slices Foreground crop + 96³ class-balanced patches Irregular anisotropic sampling drops thin/small lesions before the network ever sees them Reproduced in A
D7 Dead label remap merging RC→ET — a 4-class contract on 5-class data Assert 5-class {0,1,2,3,4} at load Silently deletes the resection-cavity class; a 2020-era assumption smuggled onto 2024 post-treatment data Enforced on BOTH (5-class asserted at load)
D8 No normalisation layers in the network (left as-is) A genuine handicap — but shared, so it is held constant on BOTH tracks and is explicitly not part of the A/B Held constant
D9 Uncached, I/O-bound per-epoch loader MONAI PersistentDataset cache Pure engineering speed: ~23 s → ~8 s/epoch (~2.8×); no accuracy effect Reproduced in A

So Track A reproduces D1, D3, D4, D5, D6, D9; D2 is fixed on both (you cannot run a fair comparison with a broken metric); D7 is enforced on both (the 5-class contract is a correctness guardrail, not a tuning knob); D8 is held constant on both (an equal handicap — see the parameter discussion below). Naming this split honestly is the point: the headline "+0.321 Dice" is driven by the six A-reproduced defects, and I do not claim credit for the three that are shared or enforced.

Evidence. The defect ladder shows how the six A-reproduced fixes stack from the collapsed Track A baseline up to Track B:

D1 is the most vivid single defect, because it corrupts the labels before any learning happens. Bilinear-resized masks report NETC in 105/105 GT-present TEST cases and ET in 100/105; the honest nearest-neighbour labels show only 48 and 85 (SNFH 105/105 and RC 87/87 agree on both — the prevalent classes are robust, the sparse ones are fabricated):

Verify. The A-vs-B defect handling is diffable directly: configs/track_a.yaml (label_interpolation: bilinear, normalization: global_max, slice_sampling: "…int(j*2.5)", loss: cross_entropy, metric_selection: val_accuracy, cache: none) against configs/track_b.yaml (the matching fixes). The D1 count-inflation numbers are recomputed in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py.

Watch out

D2, D7, and D8 are not A/B knobs. If someone counts "nine fixes → +0.321 Dice", correct them: the delta comes from the six A-reproduced defects. D2 and D7 are correctness prerequisites shared by both tracks, and D8 is a deliberate shared handicap.

Interview question

"Name three defects and why each matters." D1: bilinear cv2.resize on a categorical label volume interpolates class indices, fabricating voxels — it inflates NETC presence from an honest 48 to 105 of 105 TEST cases. D4: selecting the checkpoint on voxel accuracy is degenerate because 0.991 accuracy is achievable by predicting only background, so it locks in a model with 0.320 mean-fg Dice. D3: with plain cross-entropy the ~99% background dominates the loss, so the network minimises it by ignoring the tumour — fixed with DiceCELoss plus class-balanced patch sampling. All three are reproduced in Track A and fixed in Track B.

"1.98M-param"#

Claim. "1.98M-param" — the network has exactly 1,983,069 trainable parameters.

What it means. A 3D convolutional layer with \(c_\text{in}\) input channels, \(c_\text{out}\) output channels and a \(k \times k \times k\) kernel holds \(c_\text{in}\cdot c_\text{out}\cdot k^3\) weights plus \(c_\text{out}\) bias terms:

\[ N_\text{layer} = c_\text{in}\, c_\text{out}\, k^3 + c_\text{out}. \]

Summing this over every convolution in the encoder, decoder, and the final 1×1×1 output head — with \(k=3\) everywhere except the 5-channel head — gives the total. The count is grouped by the feature width at which the parameters live; the deepest two stages (widths 64 and 256) dominate because parameter count scales with the product of adjacent widths.

Feature width (channels) Trainable params
16 1,328
32 18,208
64 746,624
128 331,904
256 884,992
Total (count_params) 1,983,069

Why so small. 1.98M parameters is tiny for a 3D segmentation network (modern nnU-Net-class models run tens of millions). That is deliberate. The original network compounded the handicap with D8 — no normalisation layers — and rather than "fix" the capacity to flatter the result, the small, norm-free network is carried equally by both tracks. An equal handicap on both sides cancels in the A→B difference: it can lower both absolute numbers but it cannot manufacture a delta, because the same 1,983,069 parameters compute both tracks. If anything it makes the +0.321 gain conservative — a bigger network would likely widen it.

Verify. src/brats/model.py::count_params returns 1,983,069 for both tracks (run its __main__ block, which prints the count for track a and track b); the width breakdown is regenerated into reports/figures/dossier/param_breakdown.png.

Watch out

The per-width buckets are an attribution by encoder stage; they sum to ~1.983M and the exact, authoritative total is whatever count_params returns — 1,983,069. Always quote the count_params number, not a hand-summed one.

Interview question

"Why such a tiny model — isn't that the real problem?" No — and this is the crucial point. The 1.98M-parameter, normalisation-free network is a genuine handicap, but it is applied equally to Track A and Track B: both call the same factory with the same config, so both compute with the identical 1,983,069 parameters. An equal handicap subtracts out of the A→B difference; it can depress both absolute Dice scores but cannot create the +0.321 gap. The small model makes the result conservative, not inflated.

"MONAI 3D U-Net"#

Claim. "MONAI 3D U-Net" — the architecture is MONAI's UNet, configured for volumetric input.

What it means. MONAI (Medical Open Network for AI) is a PyTorch-based framework for medical imaging that ships vetted network, transform, and metric implementations; using its UNet means the architecture is a standard, auditable building block rather than bespoke code. The U-Net itself — an encoder that halves spatial resolution while doubling feature width, a symmetric decoder, and skip connections that reunite fine detail with deep context — is derived from first principles in the companion explainer (see §11). Here the exact instantiation is:

spatial_dims = 3, in_channels = 3, out_channels = 5,
channels = (16, 32, 64, 128, 256), strides = (2, 2, 2, 2),
num_res_units = 0, dropout = 0.1

in_channels = 3 are the three retained modalities (t2f, t1c, t2w — native t1n dropped, matching the reference); out_channels = 5 are background plus the four tumour classes (NETC, SNFH, ET, RC); num_res_units = 0 makes it a plain (non-residual) U-Net.

Verify. This block lives once, in configs/base.yaml under model:, and is consumed by src/brats/model.py::build_model.

Interview question

"Why MONAI, and why a plain U-Net with no residual units?" MONAI gives standard, tested implementations of the network, transforms, and the DiceMetric — so the comparison rests on vetted components, not code I might have gotten subtly wrong. num_res_units = 0 keeps the network faithful to the small, plain reference architecture; adding residual units would have been an architecture change, and the whole design holds the architecture fixed so the delta belongs to the pipeline.

"held byte-identical"#

Claim. "held byte-identical across the two tracks" — the architecture is not "similar" between tracks; it is the same object, built from the same config block by the same factory.

What it means. Both tracks call build_model(cfg) in src/brats/model.py, and both cfg['model'] sections resolve to the single model: block in configs/base.yaml via defaults: base.yaml. Neither track_a.yaml nor track_b.yaml overrides a single architecture key. Everything that differs between the tracks lives in the pipeline — loss, resampling, normalisation, sampling, selection, caching — never in the network. Laid out as a control table:

Row Track A Track B Same?
Architecture config UNet 16-32-64-128-256, strides 2/2/2/2, num_res_units=0, dropout 0.1 UNet 16-32-64-128-256, strides 2/2/2/2, num_res_units=0, dropout 0.1 IDENTICAL
Loss plain cross_entropy (D3) DiceCELoss(include_background=False) differs
Label resampling bilinear (D1) nearest differs
Normalization global_max, X/max(X) (D5) z-score per-modality, nonzero (D5 fix) differs
Sampling slice stride int(j·2.5), 128×128×48 whole volume (D6) 96³ class-balanced patches (D3/D6 fix) differs
Checkpoint metric val_accuracy (D4) mean_fg_dice (D4 fix) differs
Caching none (D9) PersistentDataset (D9 fix) differs

The top row is byte-identical; every other row is a pipeline knob. Because the architecture keys are defined once and inherited, there is literally no place for the two networks to diverge — the 1,983,069-parameter count printed for track a equals the count printed for track b.

Verify. Diff configs/track_a.yaml against configs/track_b.yaml: neither file contains a model: key, so both inherit base.yaml untouched. Then run src/brats/model.py's __main__, which builds and counts both tracks and prints the identical 1,983,069.

Interview question

"Prove the architecture was byte-identical." The model: block exists in exactly one file, configs/base.yaml. Both track_a.yaml and track_b.yaml declare defaults: base.yaml and override only pipeline keys (loss, interpolation, normalization, sampling, metric, cache) — grep them and you'll find no model: key in either. Both tracks pass their merged config to the same build_model factory, and count_params returns 1,983,069 for both. Same file, same factory, same count: identical by construction, not by inspection.

"the two tracks"#

Claim. "the two tracks" — the entire study is a single controlled A/B.

What it means. Track A is the faithful reproduction: it deliberately re-commits defects D1, D3, D4, D5, D6, D9 and is designed to fail in a documented way — validation voxel accuracy 0.991 masking a mean-fg Dice of just 0.320 and NETC Dice of 0.009, with the best (accuracy-selected) checkpoint at epochs 18–22. Track B applies all the fixes: val accuracy 0.995, mean-fg Dice 0.682, checkpoints at epochs 64–72. Both share the enforced 5-class contract (D7), the correct metric (D2), and the identical handicapped network (D8, and the 1.98M parameters). The gap between them — held-out TEST mean-fg Dice 0.349 → 0.670, Δ = +0.321 — is thus attributable to the pipeline fixes and to nothing about the model, because the model was the controlled variable throughout.

Watch out

These are voxel-wise Dice scores, not the BraTS lesion-wise score — internally consistent for this A/B but not comparable to challenge leaderboards. And the ±SD is over 3 seeds on one fixed 105-case test split: it measures reproducibility, not population generalization.

Interview question

"In one breath, what makes this a clean experiment?" One independent variable — the six A-reproduced pipeline defects — moved between Track A and Track B, while the network was held byte-identical (same base.yaml model: block, same build_model, same 1,983,069 parameters) and the metric and 5-class contract were fixed on both sides. So the +0.321 Dice delta is caused by the fixes, not by anything I changed about the model — because I changed nothing about the model.

4. Bullet 4 — "Lifted held-out mean foreground Dice from 0.349 to 0.670 (+0.321 ± 0.013, 3 seeds); rarest class +0.457"#

This is the payoff line of the entry: a single number that says the nine fixes worked. Every token in it is load-bearing — held-out (not train), foreground (not the easy background), mean over four classes (not cherry-picked), ±0.013 over 3 seeds (reproducible, not a lucky run), and rarest class +0.457 (the hardest class moved the most). This section defends each in turn, and — because honesty is part of the defense — states plainly what the number is not: it is a voxel-wise, single-split, small-model result, and the delta is the claim, never the level.

Watch out — the caveat that governs the whole number

Every Dice figure below is voxel-wise Dice, not the BraTS lesion-wise challenge score. The numbers are internally consistent for an A/B comparison but are not comparable to leaderboards. Quote the delta (+0.321), not the level (0.670). See §5 for the full limitations ledger.

"held-out"#

Claim: "held-out" mean foreground Dice. The result is measured on the test split of 105 cases that was carved out at the very start and never touched again — not for training, not for early stopping, not for checkpoint selection, not for hyper-parameter choices.

What it means. The 700 curated cases were partitioned once, deterministically at seed 42, into three disjoint sets: 490 train / 105 validation / 105 test (70/15/15), stratified by resection-cavity presence so that RC appears in 82.9% of cases in all three partitions identically (see §2 for the stratification defense). The three partitions play three non-overlapping roles:

Partition Cases Role Touched during model choice?
Train 490 Fit network weights Yes — gradients
Validation 105 Select the best epoch / checkpoint Yes — model selection
Test 105 Report the final number No — opened once, at the end

Because the test set influenced nothing — no weight, no epoch pick, no threshold — its Dice is an honest generalization estimate: it answers "how does this model do on cases it has never had any causal contact with?" A number computed on train would measure memorization; a number computed on validation would be optimistically biased because validation chose the checkpoint. Only the held-out test set is free of both leaks. Critically, this discipline is applied identically to both tracks — Track A and Track B are scored on the same 105 cases — so the comparison is fair by construction.

Verify. The frozen split is committed at reports/splits.json (seed 42, the 105 test IDs enumerated); per-seed test scores are in reports/eval_a_s{0,1,2}.json and reports/eval_b_s{0,1,2}.json, aggregated in reports/dossier_facts.json.

Interview question

"How do I know you didn't tune on the test set?" The split is fixed once at seed 42 and written to reports/splits.json before any training; checkpoint selection reads only validation Dice (04_evaluate.py selects on val mean-fg — that is the D4 fix), and the 105 test IDs are loaded only by the final evaluation pass. There is no code path in which a test case affects a weight, an epoch, or a threshold. You can diff the test IDs against the train/val IDs in splits.json and confirm the three sets are disjoint.

"mean foreground Dice"#

Claim: "mean foreground Dice". The headline metric is the Dice coefficient, averaged over the four tumour (foreground) classes, with the background class excluded.

What it means. Dice measures spatial overlap between the predicted mask \(P\) and the ground-truth mask \(G\) for a class:

\[\text{Dice} = \frac{2\,|P \cap G|}{|P| + |G|} \in [0, 1],\]

where 1 is perfect overlap and 0 is none (the full derivation and its relation to the F1 score live in the explainer §13). Two qualifiers make the metric honest:

  • "foreground" = exclude class 0 (background). Background is ~99% of every volume, so including it would let a model that predicts "all background" score enormously well — exactly the pathology behind Track A's 0.991 voxel accuracy (§3, D4). Foreground Dice refuses that free lunch.
  • "mean" = the unweighted average over the four tumour classes {NETC, SNFH, ET, RC}. Unweighted means a rare class counts as much as a common one — so a model cannot hide a failed rare class behind a strong common one.

The worked class-averages that produce the two headline numbers:

\[\text{Track A} = \frac{0.009 + 0.683 + 0.299 + 0.403}{4} = \frac{1.394}{4} = 0.349,\]
\[\text{Track B} = \frac{0.466 + 0.870 + 0.650 + 0.694}{4} = \frac{2.680}{4} = 0.670.\]

Verify. Metric is MONAI's DiceMetric with background excluded (the D2 fix — the original per-class Dice had a shape/index bug); the four per-class means feeding each average are in reports/dossier_facts.json under per_class, and the aggregate A_mean = 0.349, B_mean = 0.670 under stats.

The one-liner

Foreground-mean Dice is the metric that can't be gamed by the background and can't hide a dead rare class — which is precisely why Track A scores 0.349 on it despite 0.991 voxel accuracy.

"from 0.349 to 0.670"#

Claim: "from 0.349 to 0.670". Averaged over 3 seeds on the 105-case test set, mean foreground Dice rose from Track A 0.349 ± 0.013 to Track B 0.670 ± 0.002 — an absolute lift of +0.321.

What it means. The lift is not uniform across classes; the per-class breakdown shows where the fixes bought their gains. Mean ± SD over the 3 seeds:

Class Track A (mean ± SD) Track B (mean ± SD) Δ
NETC (necrotic core) 0.009 ± 0.008 0.466 ± 0.004 +0.457
SNFH (oedema / FLAIR) 0.683 ± 0.017 0.870 ± 0.003 +0.187
ET (enhancing tumour) 0.299 ± 0.033 0.650 ± 0.007 +0.351
RC (resection cavity) 0.403 ± 0.026 0.694 ± 0.002 +0.291
Mean foreground 0.349 ± 0.013 0.670 ± 0.002 +0.321

Two things stand out. First, every class improves — this is not a trade where one class is sacrificed for another. Second, Track B's per-seed SDs collapse (0.002–0.007) relative to Track A's (0.008–0.033): the fixed pipeline is not just better on average, it is far more stable across seeds.

Numbers convince the head; overlays convince the eye. The qualitative panels below show, per case, the ground-truth mask against Track A's and Track B's predictions on held-out slices — the collapse of Track A's rare-class structure and its recovery under Track B are visible directly.

Verify. Per-class and aggregate means in reports/dossier_facts.json; per-seed source scores in reports/eval_{a,b}_s{0,1,2}.json; the figures are regenerated deterministically by scripts/dossier_figures.py; overlays are rendered from the committed test predictions.

Interview question

"0.67 is far below the 0.9 you see on leaderboards — isn't this weak?" Three answers. (1) These are voxel-wise Dice, not the BraTS lesion-wise score the leaderboards report — different denominators, not comparable. (2) The model is a deliberate handicap: a 1.98M-param U-Net, three modalities, on a resampled 182×218×182 mirror, held byte-identical across both arms so that the only thing that changes is the pipeline. (3) The result is the delta, not the level — +0.321 with the network frozen is causal evidence about the pipeline; pushing the absolute number to 0.9 would mean a bigger model and lesion-wise scoring, which would destroy the controlled comparison. The level is intentionally low so the delta can be clean.

"(+0.321 ± 0.013, 3 seeds)"#

Claim: "(+0.321 ± 0.013, 3 seeds)". The lift is +0.321, and the ±0.013 is the standard deviation of the delta computed across 3 independent training seeds.

What it means. For each seed \(i \in \{0,1,2\}\) both tracks were trained from scratch and the paired difference \(\Delta_i = B_i - A_i\) computed on the same test set. The three per-seed deltas are:

\[\Delta = [0.332,\; 0.325,\; 0.307], \qquad \bar{\Delta} = 0.321, \qquad \mathrm{SD} = 0.013.\]

The full inferential statistics on the paired deltas (standard error \(\text{SE} = \text{SD}/\sqrt{3} = 0.01286/\sqrt{3} = 0.0074\), using the unrounded SD):

  • 95% t-CI (df = 2, \(t_{\text{crit}} = 4.303\)): \(0.321 \pm 4.303 \times 0.0074 = [0.290,\; 0.353]\) — excludes 0.
  • Paired t-test: \(t(2) = 43.3\), \(p = 0.0005\) (two-sided).
  • Effect size: Cohen's \(d = 25\).

An effect size of 25 and a CI that clears zero by a wide margin say the improvement is not seed noise. But — and this is the honest boundary — these statistics describe reproducibility across seeds on one fixed test split, not generalization to a new population. The t-test's "sample" is three random seeds, so it answers "would I get this lift again if I re-ran training?" (yes, overwhelmingly). It does not answer "would this lift hold on a different 105 patients?" — for that the relevant, un-quantified uncertainty is the single fixed test set itself. With one split, that population variance is unestimated; the tight CI is a statement about training determinism, not about patients.

Verify. Every statistic is computed in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py and dumped to reports/dossier_facts.json (per_seed_delta, delta_mean, delta_sd, ci95, paired_t, p_two_sided, cohens_d); the per-seed inputs are the six reports/eval_{a,b}_s{0,1,2}.json files.

Watch out — what n = 3 does and does not buy

The n in "n = 3" is seeds, not patients. It licenses "the lift reproduces across training runs," not "the lift generalizes to new populations." Never let the small, tidy CI be read as clinical-grade uncertainty — the real uncertainty lives in the single 105-case split, and it is not quantified here.

Interview question

"n = 3 is tiny — is +0.321 real?" As a claim about reproducibility, yes and emphatically: three from-scratch reruns give deltas of 0.332, 0.325, 0.307 — a 95% CI of [0.290, 0.353] that clears zero, and Cohen's d = 25. But I'd correct the framing: n = 3 is small for a population claim, and I don't make one. The honest statement is "the lift is robust to seed"; the un-estimated risk is the fixed test split, which I flag rather than paper over (§5). If I wanted a population claim I'd need k-fold or multiple splits, which I state as future work, not as a result.

"rarest class +0.457"#

Claim: "rarest class +0.457". The NETC class (non-enhancing tumour core, the necrotic core) — the rarest of the four — improved the most, from 0.009 to 0.466, a gain of +0.457.

What it means. NETC is rare in two senses. Physically, on the faithfully-labelled test set it is GT-present in only 48 of 105 cases, and where present it is often a handful of voxels. That rarity is exactly why Track A scores essentially 0.009 — a near-total failure. Track A's loss is plain cross-entropy (defect D3): a per-voxel loss has no incentive to find a few dozen NETC voxels when predicting "background/oedema" everywhere already drives the loss down. The gradient signal from a rare class is swamped. The rarest class is therefore the one a badly-configured pipeline abandons first.

The fixes target precisely that failure mode: DiceCELoss (which is overlap-based and does not vanish for a small structure) plus class-balanced 96³ patch sampling (D3/D6), which oversamples patches containing rare classes so NETC actually appears in the gradient. Because Track A started near zero, it also has the most room to recover — hence the rarest class posts the largest delta. The mechanism and the magnitude line up: the class the plain pipeline neglected is the class the fixes were built to rescue.

There is a second, sharper twist that ties back to D1. Track A's labels are resized with bilinear cv2.resize on the integer label volume, which interpolates class indices and invents voxels. The consequence for counting:

Class Track A (bilinear) reports GT-present Faithful (nearest-neighbour) GT-present
NETC 105 / 105 48 / 105
ET 100 / 105 85 / 105
SNFH 105 / 105 105 / 105
RC 87 / 87 87 / 87

So Track A doesn't merely segment NETC badly — its very inputs claim NETC is present in all 105 cases when the truth is 48. The pipeline is being scored against a label field that has been inflated by an interpolation bug, which is part of why its NETC Dice is a meaningless 0.009 rather than an honestly-failed one. The D1 fix (nearest-neighbour resampling) is what makes the 48 the real denominator, and the class-balanced loss is what lets Track B reach 0.466 against it.

Verify. NETC A→B means and the countA = 105 vs countB = 48 inflation are in reports/dossier_facts.json under per_class.NETC; the label-count comparison is in reports/labels_summary.json; the D1 mechanism sits at the bottom of the defect ladder (§ explainer, figures/diagrams/s20_defect_ladder.png).

Interview question

"Why does the rarest class gain the most?" Two compounding reasons. Mechanistically, plain cross-entropy (Track A's loss) has no incentive to find a handful of NETC voxels — it minimizes just as well by predicting background everywhere — so NETC collapses to 0.009; the fixes (DiceCELoss + class-balanced patch sampling) are aimed at exactly that failure, and a class starting near zero has the most headroom, so it posts the biggest delta (+0.457). Additionally, Track A's bilinear label resize (D1) inflates NETC to appear in 105/105 cases when it truly appears in 48 — so the fix isn't only better segmentation, it's scoring against honest labels. The rarest class is the one a broken pipeline neglects first and a fixed pipeline recovers most.

5. Cross-examination: the hard questions, answered#

The four preceding sections defended the CV entry phrase by phrase. This one does the opposite job: it invites the attack. An interviewer who knows the field will not ask you to explain your method — they will try to break it. Below are the seven sharpest objections this project draws, each answered honestly, with the exact number, the figure, and the committed artifact where it can be checked. Where the honest answer is a limitation, it is stated as a limitation and not smoothed over. The governing principle throughout: the deliverable is a controlled +0.321 delta with the architecture held identical, not an absolute Dice level — so most attacks on the absolute level miss the claim, and the two attacks that land (single test split; a resampled mirror) are conceded openly.

"0.67 Dice is low — a competition model gets 0.9"#

The claim under attack is the headline number: Track B reaches mean foreground Dice 0.670 ± 0.002 on the held-out test set (n_test = 105), lifted from Track A's 0.349 ± 0.013, a delta of +0.321 ± 0.013. Against a challenge leaderboard reporting ~0.9, 0.67 looks weak.

What the objection misunderstands is which quantity is the product. Three facts make the absolute level non-comparable, and none of them touch the delta. First, the metric is voxel-wise Dice, not the BraTS lesion-wise score — a different denominator (per-lesion connected-component matching versus per-voxel overlap), so it is internally consistent for an A/B but cannot be laid next to a leaderboard number. Second, the setup is deliberately austere: a single MONAI 3D U-Net of 1,983,069 trainable parameters, no test-time augmentation, no ensembling, fits inside an 8 GB RTX 4060 laptop GPU, trained on a resampled 700-case community mirror at 182×218×182 rather than a curated native-resolution challenge corpus. Competition scores of 0.9 come from large ensembles with TTA on native-geometry data — a different object entirely. Third, and decisively, the architecture is held byte-identical across both tracks, so the +0.321 is attributable to the pipeline fixes alone; the model is a constant, not a variable, and its absolute ceiling is irrelevant to a causal claim about the pipeline.

The parameter budget makes the "small model" point concrete rather than rhetorical:

And the deliverable — the delta with its interval — is the thing to look at, not the height of either bar:

Verify: the absolute levels and the delta are recomputed in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py; the parameter count is asserted at model-build time (out_channels = 5, channels (16,32,64,128,256), num_res_units = 0) and reproduced in reports/figures/dossier/param_breakdown.png.

Interview question

"Your best model is 0.67 and the leaderboard is 0.9 — isn't this just a weak result?" The 0.67 is voxel-wise Dice from a 1.98M-parameter single model with no TTA or ensembling on an 8 GB RTX 4060 laptop GPU over a resampled mirror — it is not, and never claims to be, comparable to a lesion-wise leaderboard score. The product here is the +0.321 delta measured with the architecture held identical across both arms, which isolates the pipeline as the cause. If I wanted a higher absolute number I would ensemble and use native geometry; that would raise both tracks and leave the causal claim unchanged.

"Track A is a strawman built to lose"#

The claim under attack is that Track A is a fair baseline rather than a punching bag assembled to make the delta look big.

What the objection gets right in spirit is the burden it places on me: a controlled A/B is only worth anything if the "before" arm faithfully reproduces a real pathology rather than a caricature. So the defense is traceability. Track A reproduces six of nine defects that were traced to specific lines of the reference code — D1 (bilinear cv2.resize on the integer label volume), D3 (plain cross-entropy, class imbalance unhandled), D4 (checkpoint selected on voxel accuracy), D5 (global-max normalisation), D6 (non-uniform int(j·2.5) slice stride), and D9 (uncached I/O-bound loader). These are not inventions; each maps to a line in unet_cc.py.

Track A is then validated as faithfully reproducing the pathology, and the signature is unmistakable: validation voxel accuracy 0.991 against validation mean-foreground Dice 0.320, and NETC Dice of just 0.009 — a model that looks excellent on the metric the reference selected on (accuracy, defect D4) while being nearly blind to the rarest class. That divergence is the pathology, reproduced:

The bilinear-resize defect (D1) leaves an equally concrete fingerprint — it invents labels that are not in the ground truth. On the GT-present test cases, Track A's bilinear-resized labels report NETC in 105/105 and ET in 100/105, whereas the faithful nearest-neighbour labels show only 48 and 85:

The strongest rebuttal is that I was, if anything, more generous to the reference than a strawman-builder would be. The reference's single worst defect is D7: it carries a BraTS-2020-era label remap that merges the resection cavity (RC) into ET, making it a 4-class model. Reproducing that would have inflated the delta the most — but it would also change the network's output channels (5 → 4) and break the hold-architecture-constant rule, so I enforced the 5-class contract on both tracks (assert at data load) and did not reproduce D7's collapse. The consequence is that Track A keeps a fighting chance on RC that the true reference would not have had. So the +0.321 delta is, if anything, understated relative to a faithful full reproduction of the reference.

Verify: the nine defects and their fix-status (D1,D3,D4,D5,D6,D9 reproduced; D2 fixed on both; D7 enforced 5-class; D8 held) are enumerated in the defect ladder and the per-defect notes; the fidelity numbers live in the Track A validation logs and reports/figures/dossier/track_a_fidelity.png; the count-inflation audit is reports/figures/report/count_inflation.png.

Watch out — the generosity cuts one way

Not reproducing D7 makes Track A stronger, not weaker. If challenged that this "hides" a defect, the honest reply is the reverse: it shrinks my own headline delta, and I accept that cost to keep the architecture — and therefore the causal claim — clean.

Interview question

"Did you just build a baseline designed to fail?" Every defect Track A carries is traced to a line in the reference unet_cc.py, and Track A reproduces the exact pathological signature — 0.991 accuracy masking 0.320 Dice and 0.009 on NETC. The one place I deviated made the baseline stronger, not weaker: I refused to reproduce the reference's 4-class RC→ET collapse because it would break the identical-architecture constraint, which means my +0.321 delta is understated relative to the real reference, not inflated.

"n = 3 seeds is statistically weak"#

The claim under attack is the ± term: ±0.013 on the delta comes from only three training seeds.

What the ±0.013 actually measures must be stated precisely, because conceding too much here is as dishonest as conceding too little. The SD captures seed-to-seed variance — the run-to-run instability of stochastic training (weight init, patch sampling, augmentation order). The per-seed numbers are tight: Track A mean-fg [0.340, 0.342, 0.364], Track B [0.672, 0.668, 0.671], and the per-seed delta [0.332, 0.325, 0.307] — three positive, well-separated deltas with no overlap between the arms on any seed. What the SD does not measure is population generalization: all three seeds are evaluated on one fixed 105-case test split. Three seeds tell you the result is reproducible under retraining; they do not turn one test set into many.

The integrity safeguard is that the seeds were fixed in advance and applied identically to both arms — the same three seeds train Track A and Track B, so there is no room for seed-selection (running many seeds and reporting the flattering ones). Both arms drew from the same seed set; the comparison is paired at the seed level.

Verify: the per-seed vectors and the seed list are emitted by scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py; the interval and its derivation are in reports/figures/dossier/delta_ci.png.

Watch out — do not oversell the interval

±0.013 is a seed interval on one test split. It is honest to say "reproducible across seeds"; it is dishonest to say "generalizes to the population." The real uncertainty is the single 105-case test set — carried into the next answer.

Interview question

"Three seeds — how can you claim anything statistically?" Three seeds measure reproducibility across retraining, and there the signal is clean: per-seed deltas of 0.307, 0.325, 0.332, with no arm overlap on any seed. They do not measure population generalization — that would need many test sets, and I have one fixed 105-case split. The seeds were fixed before the runs and applied identically to both arms, so there is no seed-selection; the honest bound is one dataset, which I state plainly rather than dress up as external validity.

"It's a difference of means, not a hypothesis test"#

The claim under attack is that "+0.321" is just a gap between two averages with no inferential backing.

What the objection deserves is a concession followed by the support. I concede the framing: the headline is a difference of means. But it is not only that. Treating the three seeds as paired observations of the delta gives a paired t(2) = 43.3, p = 0.0005 (two-sided), Cohen's d = 25, with SE = 0.0074 and a 95% t-CI (df = 2) of [0.290, 0.353] that excludes zero. Those are supportive statistics, and they are enormous — but their size is exactly why they must be read carefully.

The honest reading is that the tiny p-value and d = 25 reflect how little seed noise there is, not how broadly the result generalizes. A t-test on three seeds answers "is the delta reliably non-zero across retraining?" — yes, overwhelmingly. It does not answer "does the delta hold on a new cohort?" The real limitation is the single 105-case test set, not the seed count. I would rather state that a d of 25 is an artifact of low within-arm variance on one split than let an interviewer assume it means population-level certainty.

Verify: t, p, d, SE, and the CI are all computed in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py and rendered in reports/figures/dossier/delta_ci.png.

Interview question

"That's a difference of means, not a test — where's your inference?" Fair framing, and I add the inference: paired t(2) = 43.3, p = 0.0005, Cohen's d = 25, 95% CI [0.290, 0.353] excluding zero. But I read those honestly — a d of 25 reflects tiny seed-to-seed noise, not broad generalization. The binding limitation is the single fixed test split, not the number of seeds, and I would not let the p-value be mistaken for external validity.

"A community mirror in MNI-like space isn't real BraTS data"#

The claim under attack is the data provenance: the 700 cases come from a Kaggle mirror (i212385nomanarif/2024-brats-glioma) at geometry 182×218×182 — a resampled, MNI-like grid, not the native 240×240×155 of the official release.

What defuses the objection for the A/B specifically is that both tracks consume the identical data — same mirror, same split, same geometry. Any distributional quirk of the mirror is a shared constant across the two arms, so it cannot manufacture a delta; it cancels. The controlled comparison is therefore unaffected by the choice of mirror.

What I concede, and cite properly, is the absolute framing. For anything stated in absolute terms I point to the official source rather than the mirror: BraTS 2024 post-treatment glioma (BraTS-GLI), de Verdier et al., arXiv:2405.18368. And I flag the geometry as a provenance caveat: the 182×218×182 grid is resampled, so absolute numbers are not on native-space footing. There is a positive check that the mirror is genuinely the 2024 post-treatment vintage and not a mislabeled older set: ET (label 3) is present in 579/700 cases, which rules out a pre-operative {0,1,2,4} labelling and confirms the post-treatment 2024 contract. The stratification that the split rests on is also visible and identical across arms:

Verify: the mirror ID, geometry, split, and the ET-presence label-contract check (579/700) are in the data-provenance notes and scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py; the official corpus is de Verdier et al., arXiv:2405.18368.

Watch out — mirror vs official

Never cite the Kaggle mirror for an absolute claim about BraTS. The mirror licenses the A/B (both arms share it); the official de Verdier arXiv:2405.18368 corpus is the citation for anything absolute, with the 182×218×182 resampling flagged.

Interview question

"That's a resampled community mirror, not real BraTS — doesn't that invalidate your numbers?" For the A/B it changes nothing: both tracks eat the identical mirror at the identical 182×218×182 geometry, so any mirror quirk is a shared constant that cancels out of the delta. For absolute framing I concede the point and cite the official BraTS 2024 corpus (de Verdier, arXiv:2405.18368), flagging the resampled geometry. I also verified the mirror is the genuine 2024 post-treatment vintage — ET present in 579/700 cases rules out an older pre-op label set.

"Your D7 says the reference is 4-class — did you reproduce the wrong thing?"#

The claim under attack targets defect D7 directly: if the reference is a 4-class model and I built a 5-class one, did I reproduce something the reference never was?

What the objection inverts is the direction of the deviation. The reference's D7 is a dead label remap that merges RC into ET, i.e. it trains on a 4-class contract and never predicts the resection cavity as its own class. I deliberately did the opposite: I kept all five classes (0 background, 1 NETC, 2 SNFH, 3 ET, 4 RC) and enforced a 5-class assertion at data load, precisely so that RC can be measured rather than silently folded away. This is not an accidental mismatch — it is a documented, intentional choice, because collapsing RC into ET would (a) hide the single class the post-treatment task most cares about and (b) change out_channels from 5 to 4 and break the identical-architecture constraint that licenses the whole causal claim.

The payoff is that RC becomes a measurable result instead of an invisible one: RC Dice 0.403 → 0.694, a +0.291 improvement, alongside the rarest class NETC at +0.457 (0.009 → 0.466):

So the answer is the reverse of the accusation: I did not reproduce the wrong thing — I refused to reproduce the reference's worst behavior, documented that refusal as D7, and thereby gained the ability to score RC at all. The 4-class nature of the reference is written down as a known discrepancy, not papered over.

Verify: the 5-class enforcement (out_channels = 5, load-time assertion) and the RC/NETC per-class deltas are in scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py and reports/figures/report/perclass_test_dice.png / delta_test.png; D7's status ("enforced") is recorded in the defect ladder.

Interview question

"If the reference is 4-class and you're 5-class, did you reproduce the wrong pipeline?" I reproduced the reference's defects but deliberately declined its worst one: D7 merges RC into ET as a 4-class model, and I kept all five classes so RC is a measurable class rather than folded into ET. That choice is documented, not smoothed over — and it is what lets me report RC at +0.291 and keeps the network's output channels identical across both arms, which the causal claim requires.

"Did you reuse the original's trained weights?"#

The claim under attack is the most damaging one if true: that the "reproduction" leaned on the reference's own trained parameters.

The answer is a flat no, and the reasons make reuse indefensible even if it were possible. The network was retrained from scratch in PyTorch/MONAI for both tracks. The reference was a Colab export — unet_cc.py's header reads "Copy of Untitled7.ipynb … Automatically generated by Colab" — built on a different TensorFlow stack; its weights are not architecturally transferable to the MONAI 3D U-Net used here, and even a nominal port would be scientifically indefensible because it would confound "reproduced pipeline" with "inherited a trained model." The provenance record is explicit that no original weights were reused; only the behaviour was reproduced, and the reference — which has no author, no README, no LICENSE — was not redistributed.

Verify: the from-scratch training entry points and per-seed checkpoints are the run artifacts behind reports/figures/report/training_curves.png (Track B reaching val mean-fg 0.682 at epochs 64–72; Track A's accuracy-selected checkpoint at epochs 18–22); the provenance statement — Colab export, no author/README/LICENSE, weights never reused, code never redistributed — is in the provenance note.

The one-liner

Nothing was inherited: a different (TensorFlow, authorless, unlicensed) reference was re-implemented from scratch in PyTorch, so the +0.321 measures a rebuilt pipeline, never a borrowed model.

Interview question

"Did you start from the original's trained weights?" No — both tracks were trained from scratch in PyTorch/MONAI. The reference was an authorless, unlicensed Colab export on a different TensorFlow stack; its weights are not transferable and reusing them would confound "reproduced the pipeline" with "inherited a model," which would invalidate the entire A/B. Only the behaviour was reproduced, and the reference code was never redistributed.

bash scripts/run_full_experiment.sh          # writes reports/results_700_seeds.json

PYTHONPATH=src python scripts/compute_dossier_facts.py   # -> reports/dossier_facts.json

python scripts/06_report_figures.py          # per-class, delta, counts, curves (± SD)
